metadata.title: Which Step Was It?
metadata.author: Amos Jaimes
metadata.note: Built from EXPERIMENT_RECORD.md alone. Every figure on screen is quoted from that record; nothing was re-run or re-derived. Scope is experiments 3 and 3b only. Week1's reel already told experiment 3's headline (+7.61, p=2.5e-57, the failed 2-5 point prediction), so this reel deliberately argues the part week1 did not: WHICH step, how the six-arm grouping reveals it, the 3b refinement against a revised noise floor, and the design flaw the record flags in its own arms.

beats.narration_text: Four cleaning steps ran on every spectrum before the model ever saw it. Despiking, Savitzky-Golay smoothing, A S P L S baseline correction, and min-max scaling. Standard practice, inherited, never questioned. One of them was costing eight points of accuracy. The question is not whether to clean the data. The question is which step, and how you would know.

props.command: My preprocessing pipeline is four steps: despike, SavGol, ASPLS, MinMax. Removing all four gains ~9 points. Design an ablation that tells me WHICH step is responsible — and tell me what would make the comparison invalid.
output: Drop one step at a time and compare each arm against the full pipeline.

beats.narration_text: The obvious story would be that less cleaning is better. It is not that. Six arms were run, and they do not sort by how many steps survived. They sort by whether one specific step was present. Everything else in the pipeline turned out to be close to free.

props.text:
The answer was not
"fewer steps is better."

The arms sort by ONE step,
not by how many.

beats.narration_text: Six arms, three seeds each, sorted by accuracy. And notice the axis starts at seventy, not zero — on a zero axis these bars are almost the same length and the whole effect disappears. The error bars are the seed spread. Look at where the gap falls.

props.title: Preprocessing ablation — six arms, three seeds each
props.caption: Accuracy percent, mean of three seeds, error bar is one sd

beats.narration_text: There is the tell. Every arm that kept A S P L S lands between seventy four and seventy six. Every arm that dropped it lands between eighty two and eighty four. The gap is not gradual and it does not track step count. The arm with nothing removed but A S P L S beats the arm with three of four steps removed. That is a grouping by one variable, not a trend.

lines: The grouping is by one step, not by step count.

beats.narration_text: So why would a baseline correction hurt? Baseline correction assumes your signal is sitting on a slow, wandering curve — fluorescence — and it fits that curve and subtracts it. Here is the shape of that operation. Everything depends on the assumption that the drift is there to be found.

And on this dataset the assumption does not hold. The distributed arrays already lie between zero and one, and they have already been baseline corrected upstream. So there is no fluorescence drift left to remove. A S P L S still fits a curve, because that is what it does — but the only thing left for it to fit is the envelope of the peaks themselves. It subtracts signal. That is the hypothesis, and the ablation is what makes it testable.

lines: so it fits the peak envelope and subtracts that.
meta: stated as a hypothesis; the ablation is the test

beats.narration_text: That leaves the other two steps. With A S P L S already gone, do despiking and smoothing still earn their place? Dropping them too gains one point five zero, with a confidence interval of plus zero point four two to plus two point five eight, and a paired McNemar p of seven point three times ten to the minus six. Small, but it is not nothing.

props.title: Dropping despike and SavGol as well
props.caption: Δ = +1.50 pts · 95% CI [+0.42, +2.58] · McNemar p = 7.3e-06

beats.narration_text: Your turn. If you have an inherited preprocessing pipeline, the useful question is not whether it helps on average. It is whether each step's assumption is actually true of your data. Here is a prompt for that. Ask it about the step nobody has questioned.

props.command: For each step in my preprocessing pipeline: what does it ASSUME about the input? Then tell me how I would check whether that assumption holds for my actual data — before I argue about whether the step helps.

beats.narration_text: Which step was it. Working notes from a Humanitarians AI fellowship — the failures are the part worth keeping.
